    Rules and tools

    The full version of what the home page states in one line each. Nothing here needs an e-mail address or an install.

    Every ceiling and every exception

    SessionOther cues per 30 min (excl. splits, hills, pauses)
    Easy · long · run-walkup to 8
    Tempo · race · free runup to 6
    Intervalsno cap — what you leave switched on decides how often it speaks. In exchange, intervals carry only the step, heart-rate zone, pace and auto-pause cues: splits, hills, form and encouragement stay quiet
    • The floor is 45 seconds between cues. Safety calls, core calls such as workout steps, and splits do not wait for it — and neither do the items below.
    • Splits, hill warnings and the auto-pause and resume calls each follow a rule of their own and never draw on the 30-minute cap. The walk-to-run change and the breathing count are outside the 45-second rule too — late, they mean nothing. So is the greeting when it recognises a route you have run before.
    • Running with the iPhone alone the rules differ — there are fewer cues, so how often it speaks comes from a 20-second gap instead of 45, a 3-minute cooldown on pace and a 5-minute one on heart-rate zone, with no 30-minute cap at all.
    • 8 items switch on and off one by one: pace, heart-rate zone, form, hills, encouragement and scripts, running-tip cards, hydration, and the auto-pause/resume voice. Splits are not a switch but an interval — off, 0.5 or 1 (km or miles). Safety calls and core calls such as workout steps cannot be switched off. Music only dips while the coach is speaking.

    How is this different from a dedicated running watch?

    Training load, recovery time, an estimated lactate threshold, a race pace plan — the numbers people are told they need a separate running watch to see. Runvis computes the same numbers from the heart rate, GPS and barometric altitude your Apple Watch already recorded. A dedicated watch does not publish its formulas, so we will not claim they are the same ones. What we will do is name ours: every formula below is a published, named one. Inside the app each metric opens onto what it means, how it was computed and your own usual range.

    MetricWhat Runvis computes it with, and what that formula is called
    Training load and form (TSB)Banister TRIMP fed into Coggan's 42-day and 7-day exponential moving averages (CTL and ATL); the difference between them is TSB.
    Recovery timeEstimated from three things: the last run's TRIMP, your current TSB and your HRV status. The screen says "estimated" too.
    Lactate Threshold (est.)The pace and heart rate of your best 30-minute (or 20-minute) stretch held above 85% of maximum heart rate in the last 90 days. An estimate read off your runs, not a lab blood draw.
    Race prediction and segment pace planRiegel extrapolation plus Runvis VDOT. Give it a course GPX and it splits the pace segment by segment along that course's elevation.
    Grade-adjusted pace (GAP)Minetti's (2002) running energy-cost curve, with the cost of climbing and descending worked out separately.
    The five heart-rate zonesKarvonen, over heart-rate reserve; with no known maximum it falls back to 208 − 0.7 × age. The calculator below is the same arithmetic.

    What a dedicated watch does and Runvis does not, written down too: there is no watch-face complication, no iPhone home-screen widget and no Live Activity in this version. And every number above is reference information, not medical advice.

    Something to work out right now — your five heart-rate zones

    The same Karvonen arithmetic Runvis speaks from. In the app the inputs keep refreshing — a seven-day resting heart rate from Apple Health, and the highest heart rate your watch has actually recorded — but the calculation is the one below.

    Zone floor = (max HR − resting HR) × 50/60/70/80/90% + resting HR. With the maximum left empty it is estimated as 208 − 0.7 × age. Reference arithmetic, not medical advice.

    If you run in Seoul — 13 course GPX files

    The GPX files for the 13 Seoul courses the app uses. No signup, no install — download them now and load them into another watch or map app. Distances are written in km in all six languages: a GPX file carries no unit of its own, and the device you load it into does the converting.

    Namsan North Loop 6.7km · Namsan Summit Climb 4.0km · Bugak Skyway 5.2km · Ansan Jarak Trail 6.1km · Inwangsan Jarak Trail 2.9km · Naksan Park City Wall 2.1km · Eungbongsan Stairs 1.6km · Dorimcheon Stream 14.5km · Banpo Han River Park 5.0km · Tancheon Stream 7.1km · Yangjaecheon Stream 3.9km · Cheonggyecheon Stream 5.5km · Seoul Forest Loop 2.0km

    What happens after you sign up

    1. Signed up — we take only your e-mail address. There is no account to create.
    2. TestFlight invitation — when the beta opens, invitation links go out in the order they were requested. Apple caps external testers at 10,000 seats. All you need is an Apple account, and there is nothing to pay: on a beta build every coach feature is free for the length of the beta. Unless you opt into marketing mail, that one invitation is the only e-mail you get.
    3. Feedback — send it from inside the app, or to help@runvis.app.
    4. Launch — the launch date is decided after the beta ends. Korea's App Store comes first and other regions open in stages.
